claims.text: The starting protective coating has a dual-phase microstructure consisting of an FCC matrix with embedded BCC regions.
The starting coating is produced by conventional processing and has an average baseline FCC/BCC phase-boundary density.
Heat treatment or another processing modification can increase both the stability and density of FCC/BCC phase boundaries without changing overall alloy composition.
High-temperature creep is progressive plastic deformation during prolonged mechanical loading.
Stabilized FCC/BCC interfaces act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Stabilized FCC/BCC interfaces facilitate dynamic load partitioning between the FCC and BCC phases.
Greater FCC/BCC phase-boundary stability restricts localized shear.
Cooperative dislocation transfer across phases can distribute strain more uniformly.
Limited deformation-induced transformation or twinning can contribute to more uniformly distributed strain.
More uniformly distributed strain reduces creep deformation.
Increasing FCC/BCC phase-boundary density will lower the coating's creep strain rate relative to an untreated control under identical high-temperature sustained loading.
Increasing FCC/BCC phase-boundary density will reduce localized shear-band formation relative to an untreated control.
Localized slip can evolve into shear bands in high-entropy alloys.
The proposed mechanism operates only within the alloy's applicable sustained-stress and temperature limits.
Outside those stress and temperature limits, alternative deformation mechanisms or phase transformations may dominate.
The quantitative contributions of phase-boundary density and local chemical order to creep resistance are not yet resolved.

Failure of a coating with verified enhanced boundary density to show either a statistically significant creep-rate reduction or appreciable changes in dislocation patterns and shear-band formation would falsify the proposed mechanism.
